We've been working on exactly this problem and wanted to share what we've learned from building a production failover router.

A few design considerations that might help shape this feature:

**Failure classification matters more than most people think.** Not all errors should trigger fallback:

| Error | Should fallback? | Why |
|-------|-----------------|-----|
| 429 Rate Limit | Yes | Temporary, other provider likely available |
| 500/502/503 | Yes | Server-side issue, other provider unaffected |
| Timeout | Yes (with idempotency check) | May have partially processed |
| 401/403 Auth | Depends | Could be per-provider credential issue |
| 400 Bad Request | No | Request is malformed -- will fail everywhere |
| 402 Payment Required | Yes | Billing issue is provider-specific |
| 404 Model Not Found | Maybe | Model may not exist on fallback provider either |

**Sticky sessions for streaming:** If you're mid-stream and hit a failure, you need to decide whether to restart the stream from scratch on the fallback provider or surface the partial result. Most implementations restart, but you need to handle the request body differently per provider (system prompt differences, model name mapping, etc.).

**Circuit breakers prevent cascade failures:** Instead of trying every request against a failing provider and waiting for timeouts, track failure rates per provider and temporarily remove unhealthy ones from the rotation. This keeps fallback latency low.

We open-sourced our approach here if the implementation patterns are useful: https://github.com/XidaoApi/llm-failover-router-demo

The priority list approach you proposed is solid. One addition: consider a `fallback_policy` config that lets users choose between `immediate` (try next on any failure), `conservative` (only on 5xx/timeout), or `custom` (user-defined error codes).

Adding some evidence here from a different angle that might shift the priority of fix # 2 (debounce + coalesce `refreshVcs()`) above fix # 1 (separate summary stats from full patches). I was hitting the same 100%+ CPU symptom on a large monorepo, but when I looked at Activity Monitor while it was happening, the split was **89% system time vs 11% user time**: If `structuredPatch()` were the dominant cost, I'd expect that to show up as user time. 89% system time points at the kernel doing fork/exec/wait/SIGCHLD work. The cost is spawning git processes, not running the JS-side patch builder. Looking at the process tree at the same moment, I had 53+ concurrent `git status --porcelain=v1 --untracked-files=all --no-renames -z -- .` targeting the same worktree So in this case the bottleneck is the unbounded fan-out itself. Even with `structuredPatch` made cheap, an unbounded number of `git status --untracked-files=all` invocations stacking faster than they finish on a large repo is enough on its own to peg CPU. (Filed the zombie-reaping side of this separately at #25883 since it seems like a distinct bug worth its own thread. 4,978 `` children persisting for several minutes after activity stops.)

Still an issue in openchamber and opencode... this is a crucial and basic feature that's available in other LLM coding platforms, it should be available here.. this is such a great product with a great subscription(in today's "you've hit your session's limit"), but this issue increases friction so much for me.

Workaround: we found that running a second `opencode web` instance on a different port (for session isolation) triggers this bug. The manifest 401 is cosmetic but the `/global/event` 401 crashes the UI with PasteTypeError, making the session page completely blank.

Our workaround: the secondary server runs without auth (`OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD` unset) and we don't open its web UI at all. Instead, we proxy session messages through our own API endpoint and display CoT in a custom modal.

The underlying issue is that the auth middleware doesn't exempt static assets (site.webmanifest, favicon) or the SSE event stream (`/global/event`). Related to #12447 (closed) and #9206.

We confirmed this bug affects `opencode web` instances on different ports sharing the same state directory. Even with identical CSP, identical JS bundles, and no auth, the web UI on the secondary instance fails to render session content (blank page). The main instance (port 4096) works fine.

Workaround: don't open the secondary server's web UI. Poll its REST API directly for session messages and render progress in a custom UI.
